m1 - coordination answer sent (msg-01M16Z2H7AMHPQ7H5RANPKPHT0). No claim; the engineer owns slice E and I review.

Recorded here because it is the part most likely to be lost in a DM:

MEASURED RIPPLE: 28 RecallGraph mentions in main sources - recall 7, align 14, interview 10, codec 9, laws 6, embed-bench 4 - plus 33 `.copy` sites in tests. Every one must declare its status, and that declaration IS the value.

THE TEST THAT DECIDES WHETHER THE PHANTOM IS REAL: infer, RecallSignature.compute and AlignWire.recallChecksum must demand RecallGraph[Checked] specifically. Any downstream API that stays generic in S makes the phantom decoration.

THE HARD PROBLEM, WHICH IS THE CODEC FOIL GENERALISED AND IS BIGGER THAN THE CODEC: sealing construction removes the ability to build the invalid objects THAT TEST THE VALIDATOR.
  - laws/AlignGens.scala:109 constructs RecallGraph directly and never calls validated. Under the
    seal the generator must start validating, and the tempting fixes for any failure are `.get` or a
    filter. A filter that silently discards is how a property suite stops testing hard cases without
    saying so.
  - GraphSuite's negative cases need graphs that FAIL - duplicate ids, bad ordinals, self edges,
    span past the end, text-not-at-span. Those are exactly what a seal forbids.
  Recommended: `private[recall]` raw factory with those tests in that package. NOT a public `unsafe`.

ACCUMULATION CAUTION: if validated becomes Unchecked => ValidatedNec[E, Checked], keep the
accumulation. Switching to short-circuit makes the out-of-bounds guard before the substring dead
code and its mutation test starts passing vacuously. Retire that test deliberately if so.

AND ONE ANTI-PATTERN: do not add a withUnits-style convenience that revalidates internally and
returns Checked. It puts a validation failure where the caller cannot handle it.
